comments.author: wolframhempel
comments.text: Before anyone complains that this removes the human aspect of art, it's worth stressing that sculptors have always looked for ways to automate work and save time (as the website itself points out). As far back as ancient Egypt, grids and measuring tools were used to reproduce figures at different scales. Roman workshops churned out copies of Greek statues in marble and bronze, using casts and moulds. From the 18th century onwards, sculptors used outright pointing machines to transfer models into marble. James Watt, the steam engine guy, even built a mechanical sculpture-copying machine that could (somewhat) automatically reproduce reliefs and medallions. Gothic architectural decoration wasn't about expressing the inner world of its makers in the way we think of art today. Much of it was produced by large masonry workshops using standardized geometry, wooden templates and repeated designs. So, yeah, using a CNC machine is truly Gothic.

comments.author: soci

Part of the progress that made its completion possible this year is thanks to this technology improving over time. EDIT: Actually, it’s a mix of CNC roughing to shape the stone, followed by manual finishing. According to the Sagrada Família’s website, this allows each stone to remain a unique piece of craftsmanship while significantly speeding up the process.

stories.summary_ja:
### 主な議論点
コミュニティの主な関心は、CNC（コンピュータ数値制御）機械が芸術や建築の「人間らしさ」を損なうかどうか、という議論です。しかし、多くのコメントが指摘するように、自動化は芸術の歴史之中に深く根付いたものである、という认识が広がっています。石彫刻におけるCNCの使用は、古代エジプトのグリッドから中世のゴシック建築の標準化、さらにジェームズ・ワットの複製機械に至るまで、彫刻家や石工が常に効率化と自動化を追求していたという歴史的文脈に位置づけられます。

### 賛否両論
議論の分かれ目は、主に「自動化された工程」と「手作業による仕上げ」の関係に集中しています。
*   **賛成派（自動化の受容）**: 自動化は単なる時間の短縮ではなく、芸術的表現の可能性を広げるものであると論じます。例として、長年の建設が困難とされたサグラダ・ファミリアが、CNCの導入により完成に近づいたことを挙げ、技術が文化的建造物の保存や実現に貢献する例とします。
*   **慎重派（手作業の価値の強調）**: CNCはあくまで「荒削り」の段階であり、最終的な芸術性は手作業の「仕上げ」にかかっていると指摘します。サグラダ・ファミリアの事例を引用し、機械と人間の協業が、個々の石を「唯一無二の手工芸品」として保つ一方で工程を加速させると説明します。この立場は、自動化を完全に拒否するのではなく、その役割を明確にdefinesしています。

### 注目コメント
特に洞察のあるコメントとして、次が挙げられます。
1.  **「CNCは=Gothic（ゴシック）である」**: このコメントは、CNCを単なる現代技術ではなく、ゴシック建築の精神と結びつける独創的な視点提供了します。ゴシック建築が木製型や標準化された幾何学を用いて大規模な工房で生産されていたという歴史的事実と比較し、CNCはその現代版であると見なすことで、技術の芸術史における位置づけを新的に解釈しています。
2.  **「装飾的建築の復活を期待する」**: このコメントは、現在の技術がもはや複雑な装飾を可能にするにもかかわらず、現代建築がその可能性から遠ざかっていると指摘し、未来の建築動向についての予測と期待を表しています。CNC技術が、 Past な様式の再評価や、より豊かな空間表現の実現を促す可能性を示唆しています。

AI（特にLLM）が税金申告業務における専門家の代替可能性について、実用性と限界が議論された。参加者らはAIを税務ツールとしての潜在力を認める一方で、法規条文の複雑性や文脈理解の難易さゆえに完全な自動化はまだ早すぎるとの意見が多数派を占めた。AIはエラー検出や法解釈の支援に役立つが、最終判断は人間任せという見方が一般的である。

**注目コメント**  
「Claudeに税務資料を入力してみたが、法律の曖昧さやIRSガイドラインの不足により、最終的には人間の監修なしでは信頼できない」というコメントが代表的な体験談として注目された。また、RAG（検索拡張生成）技術や専用ルールベースモデルの導入について言及する意見もあり、将来的な改善の可能性が期待される。

・主な議論点
コミュニティの議論の中心は、大腸癌の発症率が全年代で上昇しているという「NEJM Evidence」の研究結果 versus 従来の検診の有効性です。多くのコメントが、20年間の低下傾向が逆転した背景に、検診の普及や生活習慣の変化が関係しているかを激しく議論しています。特に、検診が早期発見に有効であるという従来の常識 versus 検査の過剰诊断（オーバーディagnosis）や生活習慣（食事、肥満、運動不足）の影響という二つの見方が対立しています。

・賛否両論
賛成側は、検診の重要性を強調し、この上昇傾向を検査の網の目が広がったための「見つけやすさの問題」と解釈する傾向があります。一方、反対側は、検査の有効性に疑問を投げかけ、むしろ検査自体がリスクを高めているか、あるいは検査の結果を過剰に解釈している可能性を指摘します。また、食事（特に加工食品や赤肉の過剰摂取）や肥満、運動不足などの生活習慣が根本原因であるという意見と、遺伝的要因や環境要因が主要因であるという意見の間でも分かれています。

・注目コメント
特に注目されたコメントの一つは、大腸癌の上昇が「微生物叢（ microbiome）の変化」や「食事による腸内細菌への影響」に起因するという仮説を紹介ものです。このコメントは、単なる生活習慣の問題にとどまらず、肠内環境の変化というより深層的な生物学的メカニズムに目を向けさせ、従来のリスク因子とは異なる新的視点を提供しました。また、若年層での発症率上昇について、遺伝子編集技術や最新的な予防策の必要性を強調するコメントも、将来の医療対応についての議論に刺激を与えました。

comments.author: seizethecheese
comments.text: I've done a lot of PCBA sourcing from Shenzhen so I have domain knowledge here. The main latency for this is typically sourcing. The partners I've worked with will get PCBA done within a day or two once they have parts. The claims here about a breakthrough in setup time also don't really fit with my experience. What is this, putting a new stencil in, adding different components to a hopper? I've toured PCBA factories and it's not like their lines are typically down for set-up. I think this takes like 30min? Also, it doesn't look like they substantiate their 2x speed claims? They "benchmarked" this, but with what suppliers? Their claims would make sense if they found random suppliers, not exactly specialized in rapid prototype style PCBA, so they're not comparing like to like. Don't get me wrong, I really want this to happen too, but the desire for this to happen seems to be making the community gullible. I'd love the founders or someone with circuithub to link to real benchmark evidence and explain why their changeover procedure can produce several days of difference.

comments.author: phkahler
comments.text: Pretty strict board requirements. They give an example motor controller, but then require your board to be 1oz copper. Motor controllers in particular often use 2oz for high current. No buried vias is an interesting requirement too. I'm not sure how often our guys use them but dense designs probably need them. Still, looks super cool and I don't think the price difference is very high for a company doing prototypes.

stories.summary_ja:
## 主な議論点
この記事で最も議論されたのは、The GridというロボットによるPCB生産サービスの実用性と優位性についてです。コミュニティは主に以下の点で意見が分かれました：サインアッププロセスの使いやすさ、生産速度やコストの中国との比較、そして技術的な制約の妥当性です。

## 賛否両論
賛成の声では、国内でのPCB製作が可能になることの重要性や、ハードウェア設計のAI革命に対する対応としての価値が指摘されています。一方、懐疑的な意見も多く、特に中国の製造業者との侪語的比較が問題視されています。コスト、速度、品質の面で中国に劣るとの指摘があり、また信頼できるベンチマークデータの不足や、実際の設定変更時間の過大評価について疑問が投げかけられています。

## 注目コメント
「サイトメイキングが実際に使えるかどうか疑問だ」というコメントや、「2日で完成するという主張に対する疑問」、そして「モータコントローラの設計例を出しながら1oz銅箔を要求するのは矛盾している」という指摘など、具体的な技術的問題点を指摘するコメントが特に注目されています。CircuitHubの創業者自身もサイトの使い勧こうについて苦言を呈しています。

comments.author: gortok
comments.text: A problem I didn’t even conceive of a year ago was whether or not a book was written by a human. This author has done nothing to deserve that scrutiny, but I can’t escape the feeling now of having to be guarded when I see a new book online with a relatively short history (spring 2026 is the earliest version of this text), as I can’t be sure it’s either “AI-enhanced” or AI-written. I don’t like this feeling and it dampers any enthusiasm I once had for being excited about stuff like this. That aside, if the author did write this themselves without AI, kudos to them and their acheivement!

comments.author: mcv
comments.text: I've been doing a lot with graphs over the past couple of years. Basically since I started using neo4j, although not everything involves neo4j directly. I've developed a number of really interesting graph algorithms, but I'm always a bit disappointed by how little use I get out of my graph theory knowledge. I've never needed a Hamilton path or do something with the degrees of my vertices. It's all just logic and intuition. But maybe I should read this to see if there's anything that applies to my current work.

comments.author: basil
comments.text: I’ve been using graph theory for years professionally. A good example of practical uses of graph theory is any routing software. It is basically graphs all the way down. For starters the whole street network is represented as a directed graph. The most widely used algorithm is the venerable A* to find paths through the vertices of the graph, not necessarily the shortest distance but the most optimal distance given all the trade-offs you wish based on the heuristics you define. There are lots of variations of A* and today most implementations would use its faster cousin: bidirectional A* which attacks the point-to-point calculation from both ends at the same time. Then you have Dijkstra which is used for flood searches to e.g. give the best cost back home from every vertex so you know when to turn back the search if you have a search budget. Menger’s theorem I’ve used in order to determine whether we can create a loop back. Basically search outwards, then search back without visiting those same edges. Tarjan to ensure we identify all subnetworks so we don’t get stuck in a disconnected island of vertices with no way out to join the wider network. A lot of these algorithms were conceived decades ago and are still the backbone of modern routing software. One thing that’s constantly been in the back of my mind is, since routing is a highly deterministic problem space, it doesn't seem plausible that LLMs can take this over. It seems to me that it's a good example of a tool that LLMs would call out to rather than implement themselves. In fact, see this convo I had with @simonw wherein he had Astra generate a jogging route. It setup a whole GIS stack and took about half an hour. That seems like a boil the ocean kind of approach and I’m not sure if that’s ever going to be optimal. https://x.com/baz_shkara/status/2099118620647305630

comments.author: elxr
comments.text: Beautiful website and a breath of fresh air compared to the gitbook/vitepress typical styles these sorts of textbooks often go for.

comments.author: armcat
comments.text: Graphs are fantastic - PageRank [1] that powered Google Search (still does to some extent), TextRank for extractive text summarisation [2], Louvain for neighbourhood detection [3] all use graphs, as well as tonnes of others like belief propagation, Markov clustering, A*, and so on. So yeah, learn it. [1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PageRank [2] https://aclanthology.org/W04-3252.pdf [3] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvain_method

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点  
参加者らはグラフ理論の実用的価値について語り、特にルーティングや検索エンジンにおける応用（A*、Dijkstra、PageRankなど）を挙げて、現代ソフトウェアの基礎となっていると指摘した。また、AIやLLMの台頭により、新しい教科書や技術コンテンツがAIによって書かれたのではないかという不安が生じているという問題も浮上した。

・賛否両論  
一部のユーザーはグラフ理論の知識が実際の開発作業ではほぼ役立たず、直感と論理で済ましてしまうと感じている一方で、他のユーザーはこれらのアルゴリズムが今日のナビゲーションやネットワーク解析の基盤であり、LLMがこれに取って代わることは非現実的だと主張した。また、教科書の内容やデザインに対しては、一般的な GitBook スタイルに満足せず、独自のデザインを称賛する意見があった。

・注目コメント  
ルーティング分野の専門家のコメントが特に詳しく、A*やDijkstra、Tarjanのアルゴリズムが実際の地図アプリやGISソフトウェアでどのように使われているかを具体的に解説していた。また、LLMが複雑なGISスタックを構築しようとする過程を批判し、「オーンにBoil the ocean」（大事柄をやたらに煩雑に解決しようとすること）のようなアプローチは効率的ではないと指摘した。

I use homebrew for my git and curl but haven't yet checked to confirm whether that matters here. Kind of outrageous that Apple's guidance is to edit the cert chain manually, and to expect that subsequent OS updates may revert your mitigation, reintroducing the vulnerability (as happened at least once so far).

comments.text: That MacOS hasn't removed from OS-level /etc/ssl seems like a big deal, affecting more than just OS-supplied git. Is /etc/certs not used by most graphical Mac software, I guess? The chaotic state of OS-level cert management, on Linux as well, is pretty dismaying. If Apple is still trying to brand themselves as security-forward, you'd think removing the revoked CA certs from /etc in a system update would be a pretty easy thing to do?

comments.author: truelson
comments.text: Here's what apple (themselves) recommends to patch: https://support.apple.com/en-us/149555 Pretty much every developer on mac should probably run their patch.

comments.author: qaz_plm
comments.text: Apple’s statement: https://support.apple.com/en-us/149555

comments.author: faxmeyourcode
comments.text: While there is no proof that anyone knew about these weak keys for the year and a half that they were trusted by virtually everybody, and there's no evidence of MITM attacks happening in the wild because of it, you can imagine the payoff that a three letter agency would have if, for even 10 days, there was an opportunity to harvest credentials from important people in high places. I have no evidence or proof, but I am convinced this wrap/unwrap key generation debacle was intentional and the weak keys were discovered and kept secret by the agencies or governments and used to exploit their adversaries. You don't need to perform a traditional MITM attack _if you own the airport_ or you _own the free public wifi_. The traffic can be harvested in clear text and we have to come to terms with the _remote possibility_ that this was going on for over a year and a half. If not that long, then certainly for the past 10 days.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、macOS が OS レベルで改ざんされた証明書を信頼しているため、git に限らずシステム標準の多种ユーティリティが脆弱性に晒されているという点です。コミュニティでは、Apple が提供する一時的な回避策が OS 更新で元に戻る可能性があり、根本的な解決が急務であることが Strong に指摘されています。

賛否両論は、特に弱い鍵が意図的に生成されたか否かについてです。一部のコメントでは、政府や情報機関がこの脆弱性を悪用して長期間にわたって通信を盗み听着していた可能性が示唆されており、その背後にある意図について激しい議論が交わされています。

注目コメントとして、Apple の推奨する証明書鎖の手動編集が単なる回避策にすぎず、OS レベルの証明書管理の根本的な問題を露呈しているという批判的な意见が挙げられます。さらに、「空港を支配していれば MITM 攻撃は不要」という比喩を用いて、この問題が単なる技術的欠陥ではなく、信頼関係の全面的な崩壊を示すものであると主張する洞察のあるコメントがあります。

・主な議論点
AIエージェント開発におけるSDK（ソフトウェア開発キット）の必要性と市場の過熱感が中心の議論입니다。社区では、既存のオープンソースツールや他社（OpenAI、Anthropic、Vercel）の類似製品が存在する中で、一个新的なSDKの差別化が疑問視されており、LLMエコシステムがJavaScriptエコシステムと同様に「 endlessly technologies with little adoption（採用されない技術の無限loop）」になるという懸念が広がっています。

・賛否両論
**賛成論**: SDKは開発を標準化し、効率化をもたらす可能性がある。大企業（Cursorなど）の投資により市場が活性化する。
**反対論**: 既存のツールで事足りるため、新SDKの必要性が不明。市場は饱和し、短期間で製品が陳腐化する（デープリケート）。「race to the bottom（底への競争）」を引き起こすのみ。

・注目コメント
「AgentFactoryFactory」というコメントは、企業の評価額を風刺的に高める風潮（Cursorの評価額が600億から1200億ドルに倍増するというジョーク）を指摘し、市場の投機的過熱を鋭く批判しています。また、Instagramで見られるAffiliate（アフィリエイト）による「skills」の販売促進を「race to the bottom」と評したコメントは、現在のAIツール市場の競争構造を的確に捉えています。

comments.author: iamnothere
comments.text: Interesting to watch the rapid fragmentation of FOSS into “hard” anti-AI, AI-neutral-to-discouraged, AI-supplemented, and AI-driven camps, akin to the early GPL vs BSD wars. Suddenly I don’t see as many complaints about licensing, and some of the die-hard GPL stans are silently dropping that position as Linux adopts AI-supplemented development. On one hand it’s unfortunate, because it hypothetically dilutes developer efforts, but on the other hand the most extreme groups already had incompatible personalities and weren’t working well together. This self-sorting may actually result in a better cadence and less energy wasted on arguing. The downside is that a lot of loud and annoying people seem to be converging on BSD land. I am AI-nonaligned (I just care about Quality) but I’m very much in favor of OpenBSD’s heads-down focused dev culture. I hope that doesn’t change.

comments.author: kev009
comments.text: These types of projects tend to have a flash of appeal, especially to people used to Linux, because it lessens one degree of unfamiliarity, but they don't seem to stick around for to me obvious reasons. It's hard to get involved with something like a BSD project because you have to learn a lot and put in enough effort to get committer rights. And then if you want to move the needle you have to do even more work and build consensus without getting overly emotional when people disagree with you. But it is the path I would recommend to have a lasting impact, and I am speaking from experience as a FreeBSD and NetBSD src committer. Also, pkgsrc is one of the strong points of NetBSD, coupled with pbulk and pkgin. Wrapping that all up in an opinionated installation (like Omarchy recently did to Arch) would be a more survivable effort. But as my friend Larry McVoy would say, it means you don't always get to drive the big red fire truck by yourself.

comments.author: yjftsjthsd-h
comments.text: > AlpineBSD is not a fork of Alpine Linux, its package collection is original (though many packages are ultimately based on aports). > Alpine Linux uses the OpenRC init system. Currently, AlpineBSD uses s6 and we intend to add OpenRC as an alternative. I'm not sure where exactly the line should be, but that feels like it's not an Alpine* then. Like, if you're starting your package collection separately and use a different service manager, you're further from Alpine Linux than Adélie Linux is. (To be clear, I'm a big fan of making a new OS from a *BSD core and a new userspace. I'm just quibbling about naming semantics)

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点  
コメントでは、AlpineBSDやAIを巡るFOSSコミュニティの分裂が論議されている。特に、AIコードの使用に対する姿態の違いによって、プロジェクト間で「AI反対」「AI中立」「AI支援」「AI主導」の派閥が生まれつつ、これまでのライセンス論争が一時的に落ちているとの指摘がある。また、BSD文化や開発体制への関心、AlpineBSDの独自性についても議論された。

・賛否両論  
一部のコメントでは、開発文化の「自然選別」によって協力しやすいメンバーが集まり、効率が上がる可能性もあると見られる一方で、過激な人物がBSDコミュニティに流入することへの懸念も表されている。また、AIコードを避ける姿勢を「トライバリズム」と批判する意見もあり、コードの品質や安全性を優先すべきだとの見解もある。

・注目コメント  
「AlpineBSDはAlpine Linuxのフォークではなく、独自のパッケージコレクションを持つ」という説明があり、命名についての疑問の声も上がった。また、「iOSの最初のコードネームがAlpineだった」という裏話も興味深い。さらに、開発への参入の難しさや、長く続く貢献のためにはコミュニティ内での信頼と議論を乗り越える必要があるとの実践的なアドバイスが紹介されている。

comments.author: jwr
comments.text: I have been using Emacs for more than 30 years now. Other editors have come and gone, Emacs stayed. Parts of my configuration are more than 30 years old. There were better and worse times in Emacs history. Recent times, however, are really good. Emacs is maintained and developed actively and there are many external packages which are impressive. Magit and ghostel are good examples of packages that I use on a daily basis to get my work done. Recently, AI completely changed how I use Emacs, and in a very good way. I now treat AI as a fairy that can fulfill any wish. I describe how I want my editor to work, and boom! it works that way. Examples: window and tab management, difftastic integration, markdown previews with beautifully rendered tables, markdown previews as PDFs, and many more. What is most important, however, goes back to Stallman's original ideas. I am in control of my editor and my environment. I decide how it will look and behave. No corporation decides for me. No corporation builds in a new AI assistant. Nobody introduces ads or tracking. This is something I've learned to appreciate over the years.

comments.author: iLemming
comments.text: 50 years old and feels more modern than any of the crap folks try to sell you "as the editor of the future". Emacs is the true editor of the past, present and distant future. Modal editing was supposed to pull users away - Evil mode made vimming better. LSPs were supposed to kill it - only made it better. Electron-based crap was supposed to make terminal-native editors look ancient with a built-in terminal, extensions, and a polished UI. Emacs got vterm, eat, and ghostel. GitKraken-like GUIs were supposed to make the git CLI unnecessary. Magit is widely considered better than any git client that exists, GUI or not. Tree-sitter was supposed to require a "real" language server architecture to get accurate parsing. Emacs 29 absorbed it natively, and font-lock, indentation, and structural navigation across major modes got noticeably better. Obsidian and Notion keep trying to overcome it - Org-mode just keeps getting better. AI was supposed to make it outdated - only enhanced it. For half a century, humanity has been searching for an Emacs-killer. All the while, Emacs has been a killer app all along.

comments.text: After a couple of years of detour I’m back to using Emacs since all the fancy lsp, debugger etc stuff in VSCode and Zed doesn’t matter as much for me anymore and I am just more productive with Emacs. But I am still using it like it is 2020. I hear people using coding agents to make crazy customizations to their emacs config and I can imagine Emacs is particularly suitable for this. Curious what are the biggest things that have come out in the last year or two, and what emacs based personal software have others reading this made?

comments.text: Hats off to Stallman. It's absolutely crazy how it stays relevant for such a long time. We should all learn from Emacs about software longevity.

comments.text: Is anybody here consciously trying to keep their Emacs configs/setup "lean", minimalist, as small as possible? I always gave up eventually because the complexity of addons, the org-mode-can-do-everything-so-I-should-do-everything-with-it etc just grew over my head. I've discovered that I like Plan9 Sam, Acme and, in general, the one-thing-well camp better. Each their own, I guess. That said, I did often like how "immersive" using Emacs can actually be at times. comments.author: codingdave
comments.text: I've been working with government entities for document management for 15 years now, writing software that does exactly what we are talking about - versioning, tracking, publishing legislative records both through the authoring and approval cycles and then to the public. I have not worked at the federal level, but with small government - school districts, small towns etc. Those years tell me 2 things: 1) Yes, absolutely version control for legislation is critical. 2) That doesn't mean Git is the right answer. Since I don't work at the federal level, I don't know what system they use, but I do know that their workflow is already based on specific changes - they will write up the changes to a document, then apply the changes and publish a new document. Those documents are posted on congress.gov. So they do have a versioning workflow and public accessibility, just not the same style as software devs are used to. I'm sure it could be improved, but I'm not sure forcing them into our working style is the right answer. The real goal here is not "Use Git". That is an implementation detail, and one that has also been presented and discussed quite a bit in my niche of the industry. Mostly, it is unwanted. Or was unwanted the last time the discussion went around. Git makes sense to software engineers, but not to the general public, and not to any of the document authors I've worked with. Maybe we can add a UX layer to fix that, but that isn't the bigger point... What we want is to work towards the actual goals: For the tracking to be more detailed, with more transparency including not only authorship of the change, but the source of the change. And presumably, some commentary as to why the change was made. Then all of that should be available to the public. If git works as a data structure that supports a solution that meets those goals, fine. I'm not anti-git. But when designing solutions, we need to start from the goals of the system, not the data layer. And we need to design solutions that the document authors will actually use, not force them to work like us.

comments.author: pcblues
comments.text: I hadn't thought of using git to track the changes in legislation. This is a cool idea. In Australia, I spent a bit of time trying to work out how to find which politician voted for what (both at state and federal level), so that when elections come, you can single out the individuals who voted for what legislation. I think AI may make this easier, but the challenge is in not spamming the "free and open" access to the online record of our legislation. So far, it's probably a one-person $50K per year job to do this task manually, and the language of the public legislation record didn't lend itself easily to determining the laws or rights that actually changed when bills were passed into legislation. They are explicitly stated, but hard to distill with regexes, filters or other analysis tools (e.g. "Who voted to stop electric scooters going over 25km/h?") If you try reading the legislation, you will know what I mean. "A complete and open record of the proceedings of our parliament" still needs people spend a good chunk of time interpreting and summarising it (e.g. the media, commentators, etc) which means it's a time-consuming hobby or a paid gig.

・注目コメント

## スペイン高速列車事故に関するHacker News議論まとめ

### 主な議論点

コミュニティは主に以下の3点について活発に議論した：事故原因の特定、鉄道安全技術の現状、そして事故防防止に向けた技術的解決策。特に、この事故が「人為的ミス」によるものか、それとも設備・システムの欠陷によるものかについて根本的な問いが投げかけられた。参加者らは過去の鉄道事故事例（特にスペイン国内およびヨーロッパの事故）を参照し、再発防止策としての自動ブレーキシステムやATS（ Automatic Train Supervision）の導入促進が必要だとの意見が多数見られた。

### 賛否両論

意見は大きく二つに分かれた：一方では「技術的な安全装置が十分であれば人間のミスを防止できる」という立場があり、EU全体での安全基準harmonizationと先進的な監視システムの義務化を主張する声が多かった。他方では、過度な技術依存が逆に人的判断力や緊急対応能力を低下させるとの懸念も根強く、「完璧な技術は存在しない」という現実主義的な見方も多見された。また、事故調査の透明性や独立性についても異論が交じわせていた。

### 注目コメント

特に注目されたコメントは、元鉄道技師の投稿者による専閉見解：「列車運転は緊張と集中が必要だが、長時間の監視作業は避けられない。この事故から私たちは、人的要因と技術的要因の両方を同時に改善する必要性を改めて認識しなければならない」。このコメントは、単純な「人間vs機械」の二分法ではなく、両者が協調する安全文化の重要性を指摘し、幅広い共感を得た。

comments.author: x3haloed
comments.text: This topic is bringing out the hallucination-panic crowd. It's perfectly safe to use LLMs to surface underlying data and knowledge without having to trust that it's giving you correct advice. Use the LLM as search technology: string match -> semantic search -> search intelligence. This is especially helpful when you don't know the right question to ask. Semantics only help you find text that is semantically near the input query. Semantics won't help you when what you are looking for is connected to what you have by something other than semantics, like causation, mechanism, or interpretation. Trying to figure out why your crops aren't growing well will likely require you to read several articles across a range of sciences, probably scoped to the specific conditions you are dealing with. A semantic search is not going to surface those first. Allowing an LLM to chain together several sources for you to read first does not require you to ask it for a conclusion.

・注目コメント: 「Project Nomad」という代替手段を紹介するコメントは、既存のより実用的なツールの存在を示しており、本プロジェクトの位置づけに関する洞察がある。また、実際に「弓ドリルで火を起こす方法」を質問し、LLMが重要な手順（弓の使用）を誤る具体例を提示したコメントは、幻覚問題の現実的な危険性をConcreteに示す Strongな証拠となり、議論を強化した。

comments.author: minimaltom
comments.text: Former tailscalar here and now someone managing tailscale at an org. Having done my own review of the vulns and the fixes as they are landing in github, its pretty clear to me that this only affects situations where you use ACLs to permit ssh into a node (via tailscale ssh, not via opensshd), but dont give a path to sudoers/root. If a user had no SSH access and/or connectivity to a vulnerable node, none of these vulns give them access. However, if you have a vulnerable tailscaled and you give ssh access as some non-root account/privs, then yes, these vulns are relevant as theres now known privilege escalations that give access beyond some specific user account. Not trying to play down the vuln (its important), but its not a free-for-all RCE that some ppl are acting like it is.

comments.author: rietta
comments.text: I am fairly glad I have stuck with stock OpenSSH that ships with Linux. This incident proves I am glad with that choice. Over the decades, I have maintained remote access through port forwarding on my router - at one point in 2008 I put SSH on port 80 so I could access it from the restricted wifi network at the hospital my grandmother was at. I have also used openvpn. I have also used cloudflare tunnels. But in the end, I always connect to hardened openssh with key only authentication.

comments.text: Somehow I don't think it's a good idea to let Tailscale handle service authentication at all. It's supposed to be an additional security layer around existing infrastructure and services. Letting Tailscale handle VPN and SSH at the same time is basically once again a single point of failure. Similar to exposing SSH directly to the internet.

I.e. GitLab seems to have a new set of critical CVEs every week now, and I have been glad to have Tailscale (plus a physical firewall) as a layer in front of it. Total stress level would have been higher without Tailscale. And before people start coming up with alternatives, I know, but they either have the same (theoretical level of) attack surface (ie [managed] Nebula), or they require much more manual work (ie Wireguard) and are therefore more sensitive to misconfiguration.

comments.author: aborsy
comments.text: There are too many features, and lines of code (probably more than OpenVPN). I'm pretty sure there are all kinds of zero days in it, with this attack surface and feature set. I use it extensively, and I would rather pay them a fee if they could review thr code. A possibility is a lock down mode, disabling risky features. I just want a VPN for connrctiviy, no taildrop, taildrive, SSH, funnel, services, DNS, node sharing, ...They are disabled in my admin console, but the code runs on my devices and they can be enabled by mistake. A question. Taildrop enables unauthenticated input and doesn't even obey ACLs. I'm not quite sure about this, but couldn't malware in a low trust device send a file to my Synology NAS, which will then automatically process it for indexing things like thumbnail, leading to potential code execution? Why doesn't it obey ACLs, and why isn't the recipient approval needed before the file exits the sender's device? I use tags, but I'm the owner not the tag.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、この脆弱性がTailscaleのSSH機能とACL設定に限定され、全般的なRCEではないという点です。コミュニティでは、この脆弱性の深刻度に対する解釈が分かれました。

賛否両論は、TailscaleをVPNとSSHの両方を処理する「単一の障害点」として批判する意見と、既存のインフラの追加セキュリティ層として有用であるという意見の対立です。後者は、Tailscaleが前面に出たことでGitLabなどの脆弱性からシステムを守れたと主張します。

注目コメントとして、Tailscaleの多数の機能（Taildrop、Funnelなど）に起因する可能性のある zero-day とコードの複雑性への懸念、特にACLに従わないTaildropの挙動がセキュリティリスクを高めるという具体的な指摘が挙げられます。あるコメントは、低信頼デバイスからTaildropでファイル送信され、NASが自動処理することでコード実行に至る可能性があると警告しています。

stories.summary_ja:
このコメントスレッドでは、AIが創薬開発を加速する可能性について、楽観的と悲観的な両方の見方が交錯している。

**主な議論点**
 community の中心的な議論は、AIが創薬プロセスのどの部分に最も貢献できるか、そしてその影響は「革命的」になるのか「改良」になるのかである。特に、分子設計（候補補薬の発見）は比較的容易だが、臨床試験や製造スケールアップなどの後続工程は非常に困難で、those ボトルネックがAIによる根本的な変化を難しくしているという指摘が複数ある。

**賛否両論**
・賛成派：AIは研究開発費用を削減し、難病の治療薬へのアクセスを改善する可能性がある。過去の試験データからパターンを発見する「低の実の実」也有。
・反対派：実務家の経験則として、開発のフィードバックループは年単位と高額であり、MLが特定した候補が動物実験で失敗する例が少なくない。 software開発のような急速な進展は期待できない。

**注目コメント**
・「宇宙飛行士にドリルの使い方を教えるか、ドリル作業員に宇宙飛行士になる方法を教えるか？」という比喩は、大企業が自社のコアコンピタンス（AI）を活用するか、それとも他の分野の専門性を導入するかという戦略的選択を風刺している。
・James van Geelen氏の「分子設計は全体の10〜20％にすぎない」との指摘は、AIの応用範囲の限界を明確にし、議論の核心を突いている。
